Ceremonial Law Abrogated
ser-uh-MOH-nee-ul LAW AB-ruh-gay-ted
noun phrase (covenant theology)
The Reformed-confessional doctrine that the ceremonial law of Moses (the ritual, sacrificial, dietary, purity, and festival laws) was abrogated in Christ, who fulfilled the types and shadows it foresignified. Westminster Confession XIX.3; Colossians 2:16-17; Hebrews 8-10.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Reformed-confessional doctrine that the ceremonial law of Moses was abrogated in Christ, who fulfilled the types and shadows it foresignified. The ceremonial law comprises the ritual, sacrificial, dietary, purity, festival, and tabernacle/temple laws given to Israel (Westminster XIX.3 calls them ceremonial laws, containing several typical ordinances, partly of worship, prefiguring Christ, his graces, actions, sufferings, and benefits; and partly, holding forth divers instructions of moral duties). These laws were a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ (Colossians 2:17). With the coming of Christ, the substance to which the shadows pointed, the ceremonial law was fulfilled and thereby abrogated. The substantive NT teaching: (1) the sacrificial system is fulfilled and abrogated in Christ's once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 8-10; by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified, Hebrews 10:14; the temple sacrifices rendered obsolete); (2) the dietary laws are set aside (Mark 7:19, purging all meats; Acts 10:9-16, Peter's vision; 1 Timothy 4:3-5, every creature of God good and to be received with thanksgiving); (3) the festival and Sabbath-ceremonial observances are fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16-17; the Passover fulfilled in Christ our Passover, 1 Corinthians 5:7); (4) circumcision is replaced by baptism (Colossians 2:11-12); (5) the temple is fulfilled in Christ and His body (John 2:19-21; 1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21). Westminster XIX.3: All which ceremonial laws are now abrogated, under the new testament. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: the ceremonial law is abrogated in Christ; the Christian is not bound to keep the dietary laws, the festivals, the sacrifices, circumcision, or the other ceremonial observances; these have been fulfilled by Christ the substance to which they pointed. The doctrine is held against both the Judaizing error (which would re-impose the ceremonial law on Christians) and the antinomian error (which would extend the abrogation to the moral law).

CEREMONIAL LAW ABROGATED, n. phr. (covenant theology) The ceremonial law of Moses (ritual, sacrificial, dietary, purity, festival, temple laws) abrogated in Christ who fulfilled the types it foresignified. A shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ (Colossians 2:17). NT teaching: (1) the sacrificial system fulfilled in Christ's once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 8-10; 10:14); (2) dietary laws set aside (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:9-16; 1 Timothy 4:3-5); (3) festivals fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16-17; 1 Corinthians 5:7); (4) circumcision replaced by baptism (Colossians 2:11-12); (5) the temple fulfilled in Christ and His body (John 2:19-21; Ephesians 2:21). Westminster XIX.3: now abrogated, under the new testament. Held against the Judaizing error (re-imposing ceremonial law) and the antinomian error (extending abrogation to the moral law).

📖 Key Scripture

Colossians 2:16-17 — "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ."

Hebrews 10:1 — "For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect."

Mark 7:19 — "Because it entereth not into his heart, but into the belly, and goeth out into the draught, purging all meats?"

Hebrews 9:11-12 — "But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come, by a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands... by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The doctrine of the abrogated ceremonial law is held against the Judaizing error (re-imposing the ceremonial law on Christians) and the antinomian error (extending the abrogation to the moral law); the ceremonial law is fulfilled in Christ the substance.

expand to see more

The doctrine of the abrogated ceremonial law is held against two opposing errors. The Judaizing error would re-impose the ceremonial law on Christians, requiring them to keep the dietary laws, observe the festivals, undergo circumcision, etc.; this was the error of the Galatian Judaizers that Paul vigorously opposed (Galatians; the Jerusalem Council, Acts 15) and recurs in various forms (Hebrew Roots movement, certain Sabbatarian-festival movements). The NT teaching is clear: the ceremonial law is fulfilled in Christ the substance; to re-impose the shadow after the substance has come is to deny the sufficiency of Christ's fulfillment (Colossians 2:16-17; Galatians 4:9-11; 5:2-4). The antinomian error would extend the abrogation of the ceremonial law to the moral law, supposing that because the ceremonial law is abrogated, the moral law (the Ten Commandments) is also abrogated; this confuses the categories of the threefold division. The Reformed-confessional doctrine holds the substantive distinction: the ceremonial law is abrogated in Christ; the moral law continues as perpetually binding. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: the Christian is not bound to keep the dietary laws, the festivals, the sacrifices, circumcision, or the other ceremonial observances (these are fulfilled in Christ); but the moral law continues as the rule of grateful obedience. The ceremonial law is not abolished as worthless but fulfilled as having reached its substance in Christ; the believer reads the ceremonial law typologically, seeing Christ in the sacrifices, the priesthood, the tabernacle, the festivals, and the whole ceremonial system.
